title: (No AI) Silicon Valley is falling in line with Trump’s attempt to rename AI
author: Terrence O’Brien
content:
![Satya Nadella, chief executive officer of Microsoft Corp., from left, Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI Inc., Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., US House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican from Louisiana, US President Donald Trump, Lisa Su, chair and chief executive officer of Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD), Nikesh Arora, chief executive officer at Palo Alto Networks Inc., and Elon Musk, chief executive officer of Tesla Inc., during a meeting with tech executives on artificial intelligence in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. The gathering follows a surge in concern about AI potentially posing a threat to humans. Photographer: Tierney L. Cross/The Washington Post/Bloomberg via Getty Images](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/gettyimages-2297269621.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0,0,100,100)

When President Donald Trump announced his plans to rebrand artificial intelligence as "[super intelligence](https://www.theverge.com/policy/1002468/trump-ai-superintelligence-executive-order-ai)," you'd be forgiven for being skeptical that it would catch on. While most of the broader population is sticking with AI, some of Silicon Valley's most powerful are falling in line and trying to give Trump the [great AI rebrand](https://www.theverge.com/policy/1008677/trump-super-intelligence-ai-rebranding) he so desires.

That Elon Musk was [quick to jump on board](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1004598/ill-believe-it-when-i-see-it), promising to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, isn't surprising. When, hours after Donald Trump declared that "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super I …

title: (No AI) Learning to use local AI is exciting, overwhelming, and frustrating
author: Antonio G. Di Benedetto
content:
![An Asus TUF A14 laptop running Hermes Agent local AI and sitting on a child’s table full of toys.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/100926_Asus_TUF_A14_Hermes_local_AI_ADiBenedetto_0001.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0,0,100,100)

Baby’s first local AI agent. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

I'm embarking on a journey I've so far been hesitant to go on: actually using AI on the regular. Giving my most personal data to cloud services has been a major hold up for me, but it's increasingly possible to run powerful models locally to see what they're capable of. Is this tech so useful that it's worth throwing gobs of money at a computer or a laptop with lots of overpriced RAM? I'll try to help you find out. I'm not an AI expert, it's going to be a journey for me, but maybe I can help you see if that journey is worth taking - and I'll be posting my way through it.
